title: Why creators are reporting AI copycats
description:
Imagine you’re a singer or dancer, and you post videos of yourself performing online. Then you see your video on another account, and your face has been changed.

This is part of a new trend on social media called reskinning - it’s often done for a laugh, and you might have seen those videos of politicians, actors - or cats - doing viral dances.

But the people who made the original videos - content creators, musicians, dancers, comedians, athletes - say they’re seeing their work being reskinned re-uploaded, and monetised - without their permission.

So how exactly does re-skinning work? And, what can creators do when their work is taken and repackaged by AI? Marco Silva from BBC Verify has been looking into this trend.

Plus, we hear from Sophie and Monica who’ve both had it done to their content.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討社群媒體上新興的 AI 影片「換皮」現象。此趨勢指有心人士利用 AI 工具複製創作者的原始影片與表演，並將其臉部或身體替換成電腦生成的角色。BBC Verify 的記者 Marco Silva 指出，這些抄襲帳號未經授權便重製、上傳影片並進行牟利，損害了創作者的收益與曝光。節目採訪了吉他手 Sophie Lloyd 與創作者 Monica 的經歷，她們的作品遭 AI 竄改且個人身份被抹去。節目亦探討了法律在生成式 AI 發展下的局限，以及 Meta 與 TikTok 等社交平台採取的因應措施。
summaryEn: This episode explores the growing social media trend of reskinning, where AI tools replicate content creators' original videos and performances while replacing their faces or bodies with computer-generated avatars. BBC Verify's Marco Silva explains how easily these AI copycats are created and monetized without permission, diverting views and revenue from original artists. Creators Sophie Lloyd and Monica share how reskinning impacted their work and identity, while the episode examines the legal gray areas surrounding generative AI and how platforms like Meta and TikTok are responding.

On the other side, TikTok, they say that community guidelines don't allow content that violates intellectual property rights.
